# The Art of Walking: On Feet, Thought, and the Open Road

There is a sentence buried in the writings of Søren Kierkegaard — one of those small, almost throwaway observations that nonetheless rearranges the furniture in your head — in which he declares that he has noticed one thing: all thought worth having arrives when a man is walking. The phrasing is his, the gendered assumption is nineteenth-century Danish, but the claim is timeless. Put your feet on the ground, move them one in front of the other, and something happens to the mind that does not happen when you sit, when you stand still, or when you lie awake in the dark.

I have been thinking about walking for a long time now — casually at first, then with increasing seriousness, until it became something closer to an obsession. Not athletic walking, not the kind performed in compression socks with a fitness tracker strapped to one's wrist, ticking off steps like a clerk tallying a ledger. I mean the other kind. The kind with no destination, or a destination so loosely defined that it functions less as a goal and more as a permission slip: you may walk until you stop walking. The kind that philosophers have been doing for centuries, sometimes quite literally, sometimes in their metaphors, and that very few people, it seems to me, do anymore.

This is not nostalgia. I am not interested in waxing sentimental about some golden age when humanity ambled through meadows with pitchforks slung over our shoulders. I am interested in something more specific and, I think, more urgent: the relationship between physical movement through space and the movements of the mind. And I am troubled — not in a hand-wringing, apocalyptic way, but in a quiet and persistent way — that we are losing that relationship. Not losing it entirely, but letting it atrophy, the way a muscle atrophies when it goes unused for so long that you forget it was ever strong.

---

Consider what happens, physiologically, when you walk. Not the obvious things — the elevated heart rate, the burning calories, the lymphatic system pumping fluid — but the subtler, stranger processes. When you walk, your left and right hemispheres of the brain begin communicating with each other at a higher frequency. Your eyes are taking in a constantly shifting landscape, processing depth, distance, color, motion, while your feet are simultaneously receiving a remarkable torrent of information from the ground — the texture of the surface, the temperature, the gradient, the presence of obstacles. Your body is managing balance, posture, rhythm. And your mind, freed from the demands of concentrated directed attention — because walking demands awareness but not focus — begins to do something remarkable: it wanders.

Not aimlessly. The mind, in walking, does not merely drift. It roams with a kind of intention that is almost paradoxical. The French philosopher Jean-Jacques Rousseau understood this. In his *Reveries of a Solitary Walker*, written in his final years while under threat of arrest in both France and Switzerland, he described his walks along the Île Saint-Pierre in Lake Biel as the most contented moments of his life. He was not trying to think. He was trying to escape thought — or rather, to escape the particular kinds of thought that come from sitting still with your problems, which are always the same thoughts, circling like vultures, picking at the same carcass. Walking gave him a different kind of thinking. Ideas arrived, he said, like unexpected guests, and the thing about unexpected guests is that they are sometimes far more interesting than the ones you invited.

This is a phenomenon well documented by writers and artists across centuries and cultures. Wordsworth and Coleridge composed poetry in their heads while walking the Lake District. Beethoven went for long, furious walks through the woods around Vienna, carrying a pencil and a notebook in case a melody arrived, which it often did, and when it did, he would stop walking and begin writing with a ferocity that startled dogs and rural peasants alike. The philosopher Friedrich Nietzsche famously stated that "all truly great thoughts are conceived while walking," and he meant it quite literally — he wrote his books during walks in the Alps, dictating phrases to a companion while his legs carried him through landscapes so severe that he occasionally fainted from altitude sickness. These were not anecdotal curiosities. They were descriptions of a working method.

There is a neuroscientific explanation for all of this, and it is worth examining, because it takes the mystery out of the experience without diminishing it. When you walk, particularly at a moderate pace on familiar but not boring terrain, you engage what psychologists call the default mode network — the constellation of brain regions that activate when you are not focused on any external task. This is the network responsible for self-reflection, memory consolidation, creative problem-solving, and what we experience as daydreaming. It is, in a very real sense, the network that makes you *you* — the part of the brain that constructs your narrative of self, that connects past to present to future, that allows you to ask the big questions and sometimes to receive the big answers.

Walking activates this network with remarkable efficiency. Not more efficiently than, say, lying in a bathtub — a method famously employed by Archimedes — but more reliably, because walking carries you through a world of sensory input that prevents the mind from becoming too passive, too sleepy, too disconnected from reality. It is a sweet spot between stimulation and relaxation, between engagement and openness, and it is, I would argue, the single best context in which the human mind can do its most original and least expected thinking.

---

And yet. We walk less than at any point in human history.

I do not say this from the perch of some impeccable statistic — though the statistics are, in fact, staggering. Urban design in most of the developed world has been optimized for the automobile, not the foot. Sidewalks, where they exist at all, are often narrow, poorly maintained, and interrupted by highway on-ramps, parking lots, and strips of six-lane road that you could not cross on foot even if you wanted to. In many suburban areas, sidewalks simply do not exist. There is nowhere to walk. The very act of walking to a neighbor's house would require traversing a landscape designed explicitly to make that journey inconvenient, if not dangerous.

But it goes beyond infrastructure. Walking has become associated with idleness, with having nothing better to do, with poverty or eccentricity. The successful person drives. The person with a purpose arrives by car, by train, by plane — arrives, that is, *fast*. To walk is to move slowly, and to move slowly is to be inefficient, and to be inefficient is, in the logic of contemporary capitalism, to be failing. We are a culture that has become allergic to the unhurried.

I feel the pull of this logic myself. Even as I write this, I can sense the gravitational tug of the productivity mindset — the quiet voice that asks what *use* is being made of this time, what *output* is being generated, what measurable result can be pointed to when the clock runs out. Walking has no output. It produces no deliverable. You arrive at the end of a two-hour walk in exactly the same physical location from which you began, and if someone were to ask you what you *did*, the honest answer — "I walked around" — sounds like an admission of having wasted an afternoon.

But of course, you have not wasted it. You have given your brain two hours of default mode activation, two hours of sensory integration, two hours of movement that has pumped blood through your hippocampus and your prefrontal cortex and your anterior cingulate. You have solved a problem you had been stuck on for weeks, or you have realized the problem was not worth solving. You have remembered something you had forgotten — not a fact, not an appointment, but a feeling, a texture of an experience from years ago that surfaces unbidden while your feet carry you past a particular tree or a particular smell of rain on hot asphalt. You have, in the parlance of writers, gotten unstuck. You have done the thing that writing requires most and that writing alone can never accomplish: you have stopped writing and started living, long enough to have something to write about.

---

I want to be careful here not to romanticize walking to the point of absurdity. Walking is not a cure. It is not a substitute for therapy or medication or honest conversation. Walking on a path that leads nowhere, while your feet carry you and your mind churns, is not the same as actually confronting the things you are walking away from. The Romantics knew this. They wrote exquisite poems about the freedom of the open road, the liberation of walking, and then many of them had devastating personal lives full of unresolved conflict and psychological torment. Walking helped them write, but it did not save them.

No single practice saves us. This is, perhaps, the most important thing to understand about walking and about most other contemplative or embodied practices. They do not produce guaranteed results. They do not work every time. Sometimes you walk for three hours and your mind is a blank wall. Sometimes you walk for ten minutes and a bolt of lightning strikes. The value is not in the outcome but in the practice itself — the willingness to put your body in motion, to submit to the pace of your own two feet, to accept that the mind will go where it goes and that this is not a failure but a condition of being alive.

There is also, I think, a dimension to walking that is not psychological or neurological but something closer to spiritual — or, if you prefer, phenomenological. The philosopher Maurice Merleau-Ponty spent much of his career investigating the way that human beings experience the world not as subjects looking at objects but as bodies *in* the world, inseparable from the landscape they inhabit. When you walk through a forest, you are not a brain observing trees. You are a body moving through other bodies — the trunks, the roots, the canopy, the soil underfoot. The distinction between self and world becomes porous. The wind on your skin is not information being processed by a mind; it is, for the duration of the walk, simply *you* — you and the wind, you and the ground, you and the sounds that reach your ears from distances you will never travel on foot.

This is not mysticism. It is the most basic, most ordinary form of being in the world, and we have so thoroughly habituated ourselves to mediating our experiences through screens and windshields and headphones that the directness of a walk feels almost radical. To see a bird without a screen between you and the bird. To hear a stream without an algorithm recommending what you should listen to next. To feel the gradient of a hill — the way your calves tighten, the way your breathing deepens, the way the summit, when you reach it, rewards you not with a trophy but with the simple, undeniable fact of having arrived at a place you could only reach by moving your body through space.

I think about this often. I think about the distance between the people who walk and the people who do not, and I do not mean distance in any moral or judgmental sense. I mean it in the literal sense of proximity to the ground, to the weather, to the slow and steady rhythm of footfalls on earth. There is a kind of knowledge that can only be acquired by walking — not propositional knowledge, not the kind you can state in a sentence, but embodied knowledge, the kind that lives in your body and surfaces only when you move.

The sociologist Georg Simmel wrote, over a century ago, that the modern individual is always in motion — but moving through destinations, not through the spaces between them. We rush from point A to point B, and the space between becomes an obstacle, a delay, a dead zone to be minimized by technology and speed. Walking refuses this logic. Walking insists on the space between. Walking says that the journey is not the opposite of the destination but its equal, perhaps its superior, because the destination is one moment while the journey is everything that leads up to it.

---

I suppose what I am arguing — what I have been circling around for two thousand words now, the way my feet circle around a park for an hour without arriving anywhere — is that walking is not a luxury or a hobby or a health intervention. It is a way of thinking. It is a way of being in the world that we have been steadily abandoning, and its absence has consequences that we are only beginning to understand.

Not catastrophic consequences. Not yet. The sky is not falling because people drive to work instead of walking. But something is thinning. Some connection between body and mind, between person and place, between the inner life and the outer world, is getting tenuous in ways that may be hard to name but are not hard to feel. We know something is wrong. We reach for our phones when we feel it. We scroll. We search for what we have lost without articulating what we are looking for.

Maybe what we are looking for is the simplest thing in the world: the feeling of the ground under our feet, the sight of the sky above our heads, and the strange, quiet, inexplicable aliveness that comes when we put one foot in front of the other and simply walk, with no reason and no destination and no purpose, through the world as it is, on the day as it is, with the mind as it is.

Kierkegaard was right, I think. The best thoughts come when you are walking. But more than that — the best moments of being fully and unpretentiously alive come when you are walking. Not every time. Not on demand. But often enough that a person who walks regularly begins to notice the difference, the way a painter notices the difference between good light and bad light, the way a musician notices the difference between a room that is dead and a room that rings.

I walk most mornings. I do not walk for exercise, though it is good exercise. I do not walk to think, though thinking comes. I walk because there is a point — usually around twenty minutes in, after the domestic anxieties and the news headlines and the thousand small irritations of the day have had their say and begun to quiet — where something shifts. The pace settles into itself. The breath finds its rhythm. The eyes begin to take in the world with a kind of soft attention that is neither focused nor vacant but something in between, something that feels older and deeper than the attention we pay to screens and tasks.

At that point, I am not doing anything. I am not trying to be mindful. I am not performing gratitude. I am simply walking, and the walking has become the whole of what I am, and in that totality, the mind — freed, at last, from its burdens of purpose and productivity — does what minds do when they are happy: it plays. It connects unlikely things. It remembers. It forgets. It opens, like a door that had been closed so long no one remembered it was a door.

And then I come home, and the day resumes, and I carry whatever I found on the walk — a phrase, an image, a feeling, a solution to a problem I had stopped trying to solve — into whatever comes next. I do not always know what I found. Sometimes it takes hours or days to become clear. But I trust it. I trust the walk. I trust the feet that carry me and the mind that follows them, going nowhere, arriving everywhere.
